records.sourceFile: Hyperhydration Induced Decrease in Urinary Luteinizing Hormone Concentrations of Male Athletes may be Compensated by Specific Gravity Adjustment in Doping Control Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Athanasiadou I, Voss SC, El Saftawy W, Al-Jaber H, Dbes N, Al-Yazedi S, et al. Hyperhydration Induced Decrease in Urinary Luteinizing Hormone Concentrations of Male Athletes may be Compensated by Specific Gravity Adjustment in Doping Control Analysis. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018.
paper.abstract: This study tested whether hyperhydration lowers urinary luteinizing hormone (LH), a marker used in doping control, and which volume adjustment corrects it. Seven healthy, recreationally active men drank 20 mL/kg of water or a sports drink on 3 consecutive days. Urinary LH fell after fluid loading, and adjustment by specific gravity to 1.020 restored values close to the baseline profile.
paper.tldr: Drinking large volumes dilutes urine and can push LH below the old 1.0 IU/L doping-control threshold for several hours. Adjusting LH to a urine specific gravity of 1.020, the WADA method, corrected most of this effect in 7 recreational men.
paper.methods: Seven healthy, recreationally active, non-smoking men (38.4 +/- 8.2 years) completed a 24-hour baseline urine collection, then two 72-hour hyperhydration phases (20 mL/kg water, then a 6% carbohydrate sports drink, each taken daily for 3 days) separated by a 4-day washout. Every void was analysed for LH (IMMULITE immunoassay), specific gravity, creatinine, pH, conductivity and urine flow rate. Five adjustment methods (specific gravity, SG(z), urine flow rate, creatinine and creatinine regression) were compared using pooled Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests.
paper.findings: Mean non-adjusted LH was 4.24 IU/L (water) and 4.74 IU/L (sports drink), significantly lower than baseline (P < 0.001), and values returned near baseline about 10 hours after each intake; the cumulative 24-hour LH amount did not differ from baseline (P = 0.87 and 0.84). In the first 24 hours, 24.6% and 15.6% of samples were below 1.0 IU/L without adjustment, falling to 3.08% and 1.56% after specific gravity adjustment. Specific gravity, SG(z) and flow-rate adjustment changed values significantly, SG-adjusted values did not differ from baseline (P = 0.08 and 0.86), and creatinine-based methods gave no significant correction.
paper.limitations: The sample was 7 recreationally active men and diet was not controlled, as the authors note. Statistics were run on pooled samples rather than per participant. Baseline LH is given as 7.11 +/- 5.42 IU/L in the abstract and first results paragraph but 7.72 +/- 5.42 IU/L later in the results; neither value is used here as the primary comparison.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical and anti-doping staff should expect a very dilute urine sample (specific gravity below 1.005) to show low LH for some hours after heavy fluid intake. The authors suggest applying specific gravity adjustment to LH regardless of the sample's specific gravity, which differs from the WADA rule current at the time (adjustment only above 1.020).
paper.athleteDev: The study measured no performance outcome. Its relevance to athletes is that large fluid boluses before a test dilute urine and can change how an endogenous hormone result is read.
paper.rtp: The study does not involve injury, illness or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Inertial measurement unit analysis for providing greater diagnostic value during the modified 5-0-5 change of direction test.pdf

paper.citation: Ryan C, Uthoff A, McKenzie C, Cronin J. Inertial measurement unit analysis for providing greater diagnostic value during the modified 5-0-5 change of direction test. Journal of Sport and Exercise Science. 2023;7(2):54-61.
paper.abstract: This study examined the inter-session reliability of a foot-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) insole for peak acceleration, peak deceleration, maximum speed and ground contact time during a modified 5-0-5 change-of-direction test. Ten elite female netball athletes completed the test on three sessions, and IMU variables were correlated with timing gate splits. The authors report moderate to excellent relative consistency, acceptable absolute consistency, and peak acceleration as the variable most strongly associated with total time.
paper.tldr: A foot-mounted IMU insole gave mostly consistent measures across three sessions in elite netball players, and peak acceleration tracked total change-of-direction time closely. The study did not test validity against a gold standard, so coaches should treat the insole as a reliable supplement to timing gates rather than a replacement.
paper.methods: Test-retest and correlation study in 10 elite female netball athletes who performed three maximal trials per leg of a modified 5-0-5 test on three sessions one week apart. Plantiga insole IMUs were worn with dual-beam timing gates set at 0, 2 and 4 m. Reliability used CV and two-way random ICC, and Pearson correlations linked IMU variables to timing splits and total time.
paper.findings: Inter-session CVs were 1.8 to 9.5 percent for most variables (left ground contact time between sessions 1 and 2 was 14.4 percent), and ICCs were 0.81 to 0.96 except left peak deceleration between sessions 1 and 2 (0.57). In Table 2, higher peak acceleration was associated with shorter total time (r = -0.95), and higher maximum speed with shorter total time (r = -0.91), while ground contact time had weak correlations with the other variables. The authors state that the IMU variables add diagnostic information beyond total time.
paper.limitations: Only 10 athletes were tested, and left and right legs were pooled after no side differences were found. The paper reports reliability and association, not validity against a criterion. Reporting conflicts: the abstract gives ICC 0.57 to 0.94 while Table 1 runs to 0.96, the abstract and some text report the peak acceleration and total time correlation as r = 0.95 while Table 2 and one Discussion passage give r = -0.95, split 5 is r = 0.68 in the text but -0.68 in the table, and the left ground contact time CV is 14.4 percent in Results but 14.5 percent in the Discussion; table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches could use a foot-mounted IMU insole alongside timing gates to track peak acceleration, maximum speed and ground contact time in change-of-direction testing, since most measures were consistent across three sessions. The study does not show that these measures predict performance change or injury, so decisions about training should rest on repeated testing in the same athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Peak acceleration and maximum speed were strongly associated with total 5-0-5 time, and ground contact time at the turn gave different information. Staff could use these variables to look for why a change-of-direction time changed, but the study does not test any training intervention.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and its athletes were healthy elite netball players. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Infrared thermography in exercise physiology - The dawning of exercise radiomics.pdf

paper.citation: Hillen B, Pfirrmann D, Nägele M, Simon P. Infrared Thermography in Exercise Physiology: The Dawning of Exercise Radiomics. Sports Medicine. 2020;50:263-282.
paper.abstract: This review asks how infrared thermography (IRT) can be used to measure changes in body surface radiation temperature during exercise. The authors summarise endurance, incremental and resistance-exercise studies and add their own high-resolution camera case experiments. They describe a fine surface radiation pattern (Psr) during endurance and incremental exercise and argue that skin temperature measures are confounded by environmental, technical and individual factors.
paper.tldr: Infrared thermography during exercise shows a consistent early drop in skin temperature in endurance and incremental work, but the results for resistance work conflict across small, varied studies. A single average skin temperature from one body region is not a reliable basis for comparison.
paper.methods: Narrative review of peer-reviewed English-language studies with human exercise, found in PubMed and Google Scholar using infrared thermography and exercise search terms for 1992 to 2018, plus reference lists. The authors also report their own case experiments with a 640 x 480 pixel IRT camera on one to three participants per figure.
paper.findings: In constant-load endurance exercise, skin temperature fell at the start and then stabilised or slowly rose. In incremental testing, skin temperature generally fell progressively to exhaustion and rose during recovery. In resistance exercise, reported changes were inconsistent: seven studies reported a rise, three a fall and one no change. The authors describe a fine surface radiation pattern (Psr) during endurance and incremental exercise, a different venous pattern in their own resistance-exercise cases (not previously reported in the literature), and an athlete case showing different forearm and thigh patterns within one test.
paper.limitations: The review uses one search string, no formal quality appraisal and no pooled analysis. The studies are small and heterogeneous in camera resolution, regions of interest, exercise protocols and timing points. The case experiments include one to three participants each, and the link between Psr and cutaneous blood flow is the authors' interpretation, not a tested result.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not compare average skin temperature across body regions, studies or camera systems unless the region, distance, ambient conditions and timing are the same. Treat the surface radiation pattern as an exploratory research signal, not a validated measure of fatigue, core temperature or training load. Any IRT session data should be collected with a fixed camera setup and a reference object to check for environmental bias.
paper.athleteDev: Thermal imaging could eventually help staff track individual responses to training, but the authors do not provide validated thresholds or a proven link to training load. Use IRT only for comparing the same athlete under identical conditions and treat any pattern change as a prompt for further checks.
paper.rtp: This review does not evaluate injury, inflammation or return to sport. It cannot be used to judge recovery readiness or return-to-play decisions, because the paper addresses dynamic exercise measurement in healthy participants.

records.sourceFile: Innovations in the assessment of skeletal muscle health - A glimpse into the future.pdf

paper.citation: Beausejour JP, Knowles KS, Wilson AT, Mangum LC, Hill EC, Hanney WJ, et al. Innovations in the Assessment of Skeletal Muscle Health: A Glimpse into the Future. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This concise review highlights innovative or overlooked in vivo approaches for assessing skeletal muscle health. Topics include dynamic ultrasound imaging, tensiomyography, blood flow restriction occlusion pressure, serological neoepitope biomarkers, ultrasound echo intensity, body composition and bioimpedance, and skeletal muscle pain assessment.
paper.tldr: Several low-cost, non-invasive tools, including dynamic ultrasound, tensiomyography, echo intensity and bioimpedance phase angle, may help practitioners assess muscle function and quality outside the laboratory. The authors note that many of these methods still need reliability and validity work before routine use.
paper.methods: A narrative review using PubMed and Google Scholar to identify recent publications on dynamic imaging, neuromuscular assessment, echogenicity, blood flow restriction, biomarkers, muscle quality, body composition and pain. No systematic search strategy, eligibility criteria or screening process is reported.
paper.findings: Dynamic ultrasound and tensiomyography are presented as feasible, non-invasive ways to measure muscle thickness, activation and contractile properties, with reliability data drawn largely from small samples. One study of 10 participants reported high test-retest reliability for an algorithm-based blood flow restriction device (ICC above 0.953), but the authors note its validity was not examined. The authors report that echo intensity is associated with functional outcomes and age-group differences, and that bioimpedance phase angle is higher in athletes than controls in a systematic review they cite.
paper.limitations: As a narrative review without a stated search strategy or quality grading, the choice of methods reflects the authors' judgement. Most cited reliability studies are small (n = 13 and n = 10), and the authors note that tensiomyography does not measure neural activation or force and that tensiomyography and echo intensity are affected by skin impedance, probe tilt and participant position. Neoepitope biomarker research is described as being in its infancy, and the evidence for MRI of trigger points is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Dynamic ultrasound, tensiomyography and echo intensity may suit practitioners who need muscle function and quality measures without MRI, but staff should first check reliability in their own setting and protocol. Algorithm-based occlusion pressure devices are described as not without error and lacking validity data, and the authors favour raw bioimpedance values (resistance, reactance, phase angle) over prediction-equation estimates of body composition.
paper.athleteDev: Echo intensity and bioimpedance vector analysis are presented as possible ways to track muscle quality and body composition, and the authors say vectors can separate competitive levels and types of athletes. The review does not present evidence that these measures predict performance or respond to training.
paper.rtp: The review mentions return-to-play contexts for localized bioimpedance, but it gives no return-to-sport criteria or validated thresholds. It should not be used to make return-to-play or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Is Physiological Equivalent Temperature superior to Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature.PDF

paper.citation: Thorsson S, Rayner D, Palm G, Lindberg F, Carlström E, Börjesson M, et al. Is Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) a superior screening tool for heat stress risk than Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index? Eight years of data from the Gothenburg half marathon. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) is a common heat-stress screening tool at sporting events, but it has known limitations. This study used eight years (2010-2017) of meteorological and ambulance transport data from the Gothenburg half marathon to identify which thermal index best predicts ambulance-required assistances and collapses. The authors report that Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) showed the strongest correlation with both outcomes, followed by the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), with WBGT performing substantially worse.
paper.tldr: In eight years of data from one city half marathon, PET predicted ambulance calls and collapses better than WBGT, the standard race heat screen. The authors suggest PET could be considered alongside WBGT, but they do not recommend replacing WBGT yet.
paper.methods: Race-level analysis of eight half marathons (2010-2017). Ambulance transport and medical records were linked to hourly meteorological data, and WBGT, PET and UTCI were calculated, with WBGT estimated because on-site sensors were not available. Linear regression with Monte Carlo simulation and leave-one-out cross-validation was used to compare how much variance each index explained in ambulance-required assistances and collapses per 1000 starters.
paper.findings: PET explained 72% of the variance in ambulance-required assistance rates (R2 = 0.72, p = 0.008) and 71% for collapses (p = 0.008), versus 56% for WBGT (p = 0.031 and 0.033). The Monte Carlo confidence that PET correlated more strongly than WBGT was 0.74 for both outcomes. Collapses were 1.10 per 1000 starters in 2010 when the maximum PET rose sharply from the day before, and 0.66 in 2013 when it did not, with a similar maximum PET on both days. The authors note that WBGT underestimated heat stress, most markedly at high radiant heat load.
paper.limitations: The study covers eight race-years at one event, so the regression is based on very few data points and the authors state more data are needed. WBGT was estimated from modelled globe temperature, and the authors acknowledge that PET and UTCI are not designed for athletes and may underestimate heat stress in runners.
paper.practicalImplications: Race medical planners could consider PET-based heat stress stages as an additional screen alongside WBGT, especially when radiant heat load is high. The authors suggest a large rise in PET from the day before the race may raise collapse rates, but this rests on a comparison of two race-years and should be treated as a hypothesis. Do not replace WBGT with PET on the basis of this study alone, because the authors call for further comparison before any change.
paper.athleteDev: The paper concerns heat-stress screening at a mass endurance race, not training prescription. For performance staff, the finding that WBGT read lower than PET as radiant heat load rose suggests a single WBGT reading may understate heat stress on sunny, low-wind days.
paper.rtp: This study addresses exertional collapse and ambulance need among race participants and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions for injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: Joint-level determinants of the dynamic strength index implications for testing and monitoring.pdf

paper.citation: Ahn N, Kim H, Krzyszkowski J, Roche S, Kipp K. Joint-level determinants of the dynamic strength index: implications for testing and monitoring. Sports Biomechanics. 2022.
paper.abstract: Compares a traditional ground reaction force dynamic strength index (DSI) with joint-level DSIs from net joint moments in eight female NCAA Division I lacrosse players. Only the hip joint-level DSI correlated with the force-based DSI, and joint-level values were generally higher. The authors conclude the joint-level ratio may not give practitioners intuitive or useful data.
paper.tldr: In a small group of female lacrosse players, the hip joint-level strength index tracked the usual force-based index, but the joint-level values were much higher and hard to interpret. The authors suggest the joint-level index may not give coaches intuitive or useful data.
paper.methods: Eight female lacrosse players did three maximal isometric mid-thigh pulls and three countermovement jumps. Motion capture and force plates gave ground reaction force and net joint moments at the hip, knee and ankle, normalised to body mass. Ratios of jump to pull peaks gave the force and joint DSIs, compared with Pearson correlations, paired t-tests and Hedges g.
paper.findings: The hip joint-level DSI correlated with the force-based DSI (r = 0.738, p = 0.037; bootstrapped 95% CI 0.147 to 0.976), while ankle (r = -0.349) and knee (r = 0.139) did not. Joint-level DSIs were higher than the force-based DSI at all joints (mean differences: ankle 34.3, knee 62.1, hip 111.5; Hedges g 1.35 to 2.49). Reliability was excellent (ICC 0.960 to 0.993; CV 3.2% to 6.8%).
paper.limitations: Very small sample (8 of 10 recruited players, data from two discarded), a single sex and sport, and peak net joint moment in the pull measured at one position only. Countermovement depth was self-selected and varied, and net joint moments ignore co-contraction.
paper.practicalImplications: The force-based DSI was not associated with ankle or knee joint-level DSI, so it should not be read as a measure of joint-specific strength use. The authors conclude that joint-level DSI values, which mostly exceeded 100%, are hard to contextualise and may not be practical for evaluating strength or monitoring adaptations.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample the force-based DSI tracked hip-level DSI but gave little information about the knee and ankle. The authors question the practical usefulness of joint-level DSI, so it should not be used to choose between maximal strength and speed-strength training.
paper.rtp: No return-to-sport data. Players' injury or health status was not reported, and the study cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Limited Agreement on ACL Tear Location Between Arthroscopy and MRI - A Prospective Evaluation.pdf

paper.citation: Silverman R, Knapik DM, Smith MV, Baker JC, Napier K, Matava MJ, et al. Limited Agreement on ACL Tear Location Between Arthroscopy and MRI: A Prospective Evaluation. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(12):23259671251397389.
paper.abstract: Prospective cohort of 174 patients with full-thickness ACL tears (2022 to 2024) who had preoperative MRI and arthroscopy at one institution. Tear location was classified on the modified Sherman scale by MRI and at arthroscopy, and the study compared agreement and examined associations with age, sex, BMI and injury mechanism.
paper.tldr: MRI matched arthroscopic ACL tear location in only 43 percent of cases overall, although it identified 95.5 percent of tears that arthroscopy called midsubstance (type III). MRI called far more tears midsubstance than arthroscopy did (67.2 vs 25.8 percent), and arthroscopy found more proximal tears.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort at one institution. Tear location was classified on MRI by two musculoskeletal radiologists (disagreements resolved by the senior author) and during surgery by one of four sports surgeons, using the modified Sherman classification. Agreement and tear-type distributions were compared by sex, BMI, injury mechanism and age using chi-square, ANOVA, Fisher exact and ordinal logistic regression tests.
paper.findings: Arthroscopic distribution was type II 44.8 percent, type I 26.4 percent, type III 25.8 percent and type IV 3.4 percent, with no type V tears. MRI distribution was type III 67.2 percent, type II 22.4 percent, type I 9.8 percent and type IV 0.6 percent. Overall agreement was 43.1 percent (75 of 174) and 95.5 percent for type III tears. Interobserver kappa between radiologists was 0.41. Age was significantly associated with tear type on both assessments (arthroscopy P=.009; MRI P=.0001), with type I tears in older patients.
paper.limitations: Single-center cohort of ACL reconstruction patients with athletic status not reported; surgeon arthroscopic classification was not video-recorded and surgeons were not blinded to the MRI scans, and radiologists disagreed on 28.7 percent of MRIs. Types IV and V were too rare for reliable comparison. The abstract reports no significant association with injury mechanism, but the results text reports one significant clustered comparison (arthroscopic type III tears, indirect contact versus direct contact or noncontact, odds ratio 0.35, P=.038).
paper.practicalImplications: Do not rely on preoperative MRI alone to decide whether a tear is proximal enough for repair, because MRI agreed with arthroscopy in only 43 percent of tears and identified fewer proximal avulsions (9.8 vs 26.4 percent). The 95.5 percent figure is the share of arthroscopic midsubstance tears that MRI also called midsubstance; MRI labelled many more tears midsubstance than arthroscopy confirmed, so an MRI midsubstance read is not reliable on its own.
paper.athleteDev: The study measures diagnostic agreement, not athletic performance or training, so it has no direct performance application. For sports medicine teams planning ACL surgery, it indicates that MRI and surgical tear-type calls disagree in most cases.
paper.rtp: Indirectly relevant, because tear location bears on whether primary repair or reconstruction is considered. The study reports no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot be used to set return-to-sport timelines or readiness criteria.
